lesson.title: Zooming Into One Row: Conditional Distributions
lesson.summary: A conditional distribution describes one variable restricted to a single category of a second variable, revealing patterns that marginal distributions cannot show.
lesson.body:
A marginal distribution answers what does this whole sample look like on one variable, ignoring the other. A conditional distribution answers a sharper question: given that an individual belongs to one specific category of one variable, what does the distribution of the other variable look like just within that group? This is the tool that finally lets a two-way table reveal whether two categorical variables are actually related, rather than just describing each one in isolation.

To find a conditional distribution, restrict your attention to a single row or a single column of the two-way table, then treat that row's or column's total, not the grand total, as the denominator for every percentage. If you are looking at the distribution of operating system conditional on being a freshman, you divide each cell count in the freshman row by the freshman row total, not by 300. This shift in denominator is the entire difference between a marginal distribution and a conditional one, and it is worth pausing on: the numerator, a cell count, stays the same kind of number either way, but which total you place underneath it changes the meaning of the resulting percentage completely.

Using the 300-student table, the freshman row has 70 iPhone users and 50 Android users out of 120 freshmen total. The conditional distribution of operating system given freshman is therefore 70 divided by 120, or about 58.3 percent iPhone, and 50 divided by 120, or about 41.7 percent Android, and those two figures add to 100 percent because every freshman is accounted for. The sophomore row has 90 iPhone users and 90 Android users out of 180 sophomores total, giving a conditional distribution of 90 divided by 180, or exactly 50 percent iPhone, and 50 percent Android.

Compare these two conditional distributions to each other and to the overall marginal distribution of 53.3 percent iPhone computed earlier. Freshmen lean noticeably iPhone-heavy at 58.3 percent, sophomores split evenly at 50 percent, and the overall sample sits in between at 53.3 percent, which makes sense since the overall figure is a blend of the two grade levels. The fact that the two conditional distributions differ from each other, one at 58.3 percent and the other at 50 percent, is itself informative: it suggests grade level and operating system are not entirely unrelated in this sample. A side by side bar graph of these two conditional distributions would make the gap easy to see at a glance.

Computing conditional distributions correctly, remembering which total belongs in the denominator, is a skill worth practicing on its own, since it is easy to accidentally divide by the grand total out of habit. Once you can compute them reliably, comparing conditional distributions across categories becomes the standard method for deciding whether two categorical variables show an association, the question the next section takes on directly.
